title: A Thermodynamic Boundary Shows How Organic Solar Cells Can Lose Less Voltage
excerpt: By testing five donor materials against 15 acceptors, a Chiba University-led team found the energy point at which organic cells keep their current while shedding less voltage — and that stiffer donor molecules help them sit there.
body:
• Researchers at Chiba University in Japan have mapped a thermodynamic boundary for organic solar cells: photocurrent can be sustained when the donor material's optical energy gap comes close to the energy of fully separated charges.
  • More rigid donor molecules cut the effective charge-transfer binding energy to 0.1 electron volts or less in several devices, bringing bound charges close in energy to free charges and reducing radiative voltage losses.
  • The finding, published in Advanced Materials on October 7, 2026, comes from simplified test cells pairing five donor materials with 15 acceptors — it is a design guideline, not a commercial product.
  • Laboratory organic solar cells have now surpassed 20 per cent power conversion efficiency, but voltage losses remain the obstacle the Chiba work targets.

Organic solar cells — thin, carbon-based devices that could one day be printed onto flexible surfaces, windows and wearables — lose too much of the sunlight they absorb as voltage. A team at Chiba University in Japan now says it has found the energy relationship that governs that loss, and a material property that reduces it without sacrificing current. The study, led by Professor Hirohiko Fukagawa of the Center for Frontier Science, was published online in the journal Advanced Materials on October 7, 2026, and is summarised by Tech Xplore and Interesting Engineering.

The problem, in plain words

Inside an organic solar cell, the donor material absorbs light and an electron moves to the acceptor material. For a moment the electron and the hole it left behind are still bound together in what physicists call a charge-transfer, or CT, state. The cell only generates electricity if those charges fully separate — but the energy tied up in that bound state also influences the voltage the cell can deliver, and energy lost there is energy the panel never returns. The long-running trade-off has been that pushing charges apart efficiently tends to cost voltage, and protecting voltage tends to cost current.

What the team measured

To isolate the relationship, the researchers built simplified cells with separate donor and acceptor layers — the donor absorbing visible light, the acceptor transparent — rather than the blended layers used in practical devices. They paired five donor materials with different molecular structures and degrees of rigidity against 15 acceptor materials whose electron affinities ranged from 2.0 to 3.1 electron volts, and measured the materials' energy levels in the solid state using ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy and low-energy inverse photoelectron spectroscopy, techniques that capture energies under conditions closer to a working cell. The team also included Dr Takahisa Shimizu and Dr Taku Oono of NHK Science & Technology Research Laboratories and Professor Takuji Hatakeyama of Kyoto University.

The boundary, and the rigid-molecule effect

Two results stand out. First, whether a cell could keep generating photocurrent depended on the gap between the donor's optical energy gap and the energy of separated charges: as the two values approached each other, the team identified a practical thermodynamic boundary for photocurrent generation, and power conversion efficiency tended to increase near it. In plain terms, the donor absorbed just enough energy to free the charges without wasting the excess as heat. Second, more rigid donor molecules showed less relaxation of the CT state, and in several systems their effective CT binding energy fell to 0.1 eV or less — the bound state sat so close in energy to free charges that separation became easier and radiative voltage losses fell.

"In the longer term, such devices could make solar energy harvesting more practical in lightweight, flexible, and space-limited applications that are difficult for conventional silicon modules."

— Hirohiko Fukagawa, Professor, Center for Frontier Science, Chiba University

What this is — and is not

The researchers are explicit about the limits. CT binding energy alone does not determine performance: how far charges spread across molecules, how donor and acceptor molecules pack together, and the electrostatic environment at their interface all matter. The work was done on simplified layered cells, not on the blended bulk-heterojunction devices that would go into a product, and Fukagawa frames the payoff conditionally — if the principles can be incorporated into practical materials, they may help. Laboratory organic cells have surpassed 20 per cent efficiency, according to Interesting Engineering, but no commercial panel follows from this paper directly. What it does provide is a map: material designers can now check a donor-acceptor pairing against a measured boundary, and favour rigid donors, before building the device.
